 O'Donnell C.J. 

 Dunne J. 

 Woulfe J. 

 Murray J. 

 Donnelly J. 

   

 IN THE MATTER OF SECTION 22(1) OF THE LANDLORD AND TENANT (GROUND RENTS) ACTS 1967 - 2019 

 AND IN THE MATTER OF PART II OF THE LANDLORD AND TENANT (GROUND RENTS) (NO.2) ACT 1978 

 AND IN THE MATTER OF AN APPLICATION BY RAYMOND CROWLEY AND  CHARLES CROWLEY 

 AND IN THE MATTER OF PROPERTY SITUATE AT AND KNOWN AS 1B, "ANNEVILLE", COOLGARTEN PARK, MAGAZINE ROAD, IN THE CITY OF CORK 

   

 BETWEEN/ 

 CHARLES CROWLEY AND RAYMOND CROWLEY 

 Respondents 

 AND 

   

 BARRY SHEEHAN AND ALL UNKNOWN AND UNASCERTAINED OWNER OR OWNERS 

 Appellants 

 AND 

 THE ATTORNEY GENERAL 

 Notice Party 

 JUDGMENT of Ms. Justice Elizabeth Dunne delivered on the 5 th day of February 2026 

 Introduction 

 1.                   This appeal concerns the proper interpretation and application of the restriction on a sub-lessee's right to acquire by purchase the fee simple (and any other intermediate interest) in  a property, as contained in s. 16(2)(f) of the Landlord and Tenant (Ground Rents) (No. 2) Act 1978 ("the 1978 Act"). 

 2.                   The substantive rules governing the acquisition of the fee simple in land are provided for in Part II of the 1978 Act (as amended) and supplement the scheme introduced by the Landlord and Tenant (Ground Rents) Act 1967 ("the 1967 Act"). The 1978 Act permits a lessee to " enlarge " their existing leasehold interest into a fee simple by purchasing the freehold, where the qualifying criteria set out in s. 9 are satisfied: 

 " (1)  This Part applies to a person who holds land under a lease, if the following conditions are complied with: 

 (a)    that there are permanent buildings on the land and that the portion of the land not covered by those buildings is subsidiary and ancillary to them; 

 (b)    that where the permanent buildings comprise, in whole or in part, an alteration or reconstruction, the alteration or reconstruction caused those buildings to lose their original identity; 

 (c)    that the permanent buildings and, where applicable, any alteration or reconstruction referred to in paragraph (b) which caused those buildings to lose their original identity, were not erected in contravention of a covenant in the lease; and 

 (d)    one of the alternative conditions set out in section 10. " 

 3.                   If a person satisfies the conditions of s. 9(1)(a) - (c) and one of the seven alternative conditions of s. 10, they are therefore a person to whom Part II of the 1978 Act applies and a prima facie entitlement to acquire the fee simple arises. Only three of the seven alternative conditions of s. 10 (Conditions 1, 2, and 7) are relevant for the purposes of the present appeal and will be considered in further detail below. 

 4.                   Section 16(2) of the 1978 Act then sets out six circumstances in which a lessee's right to acquire the fee simple shall be restricted. When s. 16(2)(f) was introduced as an amendment to the 1978 Act by s. 76(1)(b) of the Registration of Deeds and Title Act 2006, it created a restriction on a sub-lessee's entitlement to acquire the fee simple: 

 " (2) A person shall not be entitled to acquire the fee simple under this part if the lease on which such right is based is - 

 (f) subject to subsection (3), a sub lease of land granted by a lessee who is not a person to whom this part applies - 

 (i) on or after 27 February 2006, or 

 (ii) before that date, unless before that date - 

 (I)                 a notice of intention to acquire the fee simple in the land was served by the sublessee in accordance with Section 4 of the Act of 1967, or 

 (II)               An application was made by the sublessee to the Registrar of Titles under Part III of this Act. " 

 5.                   This subsection therefore prohibits the acquisition of the fee simple by a sub-lessee in circumstances where the person holding the superior leasehold interest is " not a person to whom [Part II] applies " i.e., a person that fails to satisfy the qualifying criteria of ss. 9 and 10 of the 1978 Act or is disqualified by one of the restrictions in s. 16. Put simply, a sub-lessee cannot acquire the fee simple if a head lessee is not so entitled. Section 16(2)(f)(ii) provides for an exception to this restriction by creating a 'carve out' for sub-lessees who had already served a notice of intention to acquire the fee simple in accordance with s. 4 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1967, or applied to the Registrar of Titles under Part III of the 1978 Act, before 27 th February, 2006. 

 6.                   Section 16(3) creates a further carve out for sub-lessees caught by s. 16(2)(f): where a head lease contains a " covenant to erect permanent buildings on the land " but at the date on which the head-lessee granted the sublease, he had not complied with that building covenant, and after that date, the sub-lessee " substantially complied " therewith, that sub-lessee will not be disentitled to acquire the fee simple by the operation of s. 16(2)(f). This exception to the general restriction can be fully understood by reference to s. 16(2)(c), which provides as follows: 

 "[A person shall not be entitled to acquire the fee simple under this Part if the lease on which such a right is based is -] 

 (c) a lease of land containing a covenant by the lessee to erect a building or buildings or carry out development on the land if and so long as the covenant has not been substantially complied with ... " 

 7.                   The issues arising in this appeal centre on a particular interpretation of s. 16(2)(f), as applied by the High Court, which purports to limit the scope of s. 16(2)(f) to commercial leases and thereby exclude residential leases from the scope of that section. As will be discussed further below, this interpretation, while not explicit on the face of the 1978 Act, was determined by reference to the Law Reform Commission's Report on Land and Conveyancing Law (6) - Further General Proposals Including the Execution of Deeds (LRC 56-1998) ("the 1998 Report"), which identified the " mischief " that s. 16(2)(f) was designed to remedy: a situation whereby a non-qualifying lessee could grant a qualifying sublease to a third party to enable that party to acquire a fee simple in the property, thereby nullifying the intention of the head lessee's landlord. 

 Background 

 8.                   The respondents are the owners of a property known as 'Anneville', Coolgarten Park, Magazine Road in the City of Cork ("the premises") pursuant to a lease dated 12 th April, 1940 ("the 1940 Lease"). This lease is, in fact, a sublease, made between Jeremiah Cooney as lessor and Annie Georgina Moore as lessee for a term of 150 years from 25 th March, 1940, subject to a yearly rent of £3. The premises are described in the 1940 Lease as follows: 

 " ALL THAT piece of plot of ground being part of the land of Huggardsland, otherwise Huggartsland as more particularly delineated and descried on the map or plan indorsed hereon ..." 

 9.                   The 1940 Lease contained a covenant at Clause 3 thereof on the part of the lessee to erect a dwelling house on the property demised by the lease in the following terms: 

 " within twelve months from the date hereof at her own costs and charges under the inspection and to the satisfaction of an in accordance with plans elevations and specifications to be first approved of by the lessor or his surveyor or agent for the time being to erect and finish fit for immediate occupation and use with the best materials of their several kinds one detached dwelling house with suitable outoffices at a cost of not less than four hundred pounds with all necessary outoffices drains sewers and other works in connection therewith. " 

 10.               It is accepted that a dwelling house was thereafter erected on the premises in compliance with this covenant, as evidenced by a recital to this effect in an assignment of 30 th July, 1940 between Annie Moore and Mary Nunan. 

 11.               By way of Deed of Assignment, the premises were acquired in 1974 by Elizabeth O'Shea, who resided there until August, 1995, when she moved into residential care. Ms. O'Shea died in May, 2018. A close personal friend of the respondents' mother, Ms. O'Shea bequeathed the premises to the respondents under her last Will and Testament of 28 th April, 2015, and the premises were accordingly devolved to the respondents in March, 2019. 

 12.               The interest immediately superior to the 1940 Lease is a Lease dated 21 st July, 1893, between Marmaduke Coghill Cramer and Elizabeth Cramer as lessors and John Cooney as lessee ("the 1893 Lease" or "Head Lease"). The premises demised by the 1893 Lease ("the head lease lands") are described as follows: 

 " ALL THAT AND THOSE that part of the lands at Huggardsland otherwise Huggartsland containing 5 acres, one rood and 27 perches statute measure delineated on the map endorsed on the lease and coloured pink situated in the Barony of Cork and County of Cork were let for a term of 200 years from the 25th of March 1893 at a yearly rent of £16.50 subject to the lessees covenants and conditions contained therein ". 

 13.               Such covenants include a covenant on the part of the lessee to preserve, uphold, support, maintain and keep the demised premises and all improvements made thereon in good and sufficient order, repair and condition; a covenant on the part of the lessee to expend the sum of £50 on improvements on the house and out-offices on the lands demised by the head lease within five years of the date of the head lease lands; and a covenant for quiet enjoyment. Crucially, and for the purposes of the appellant's argument herein, the 1893 Lease contains no covenant on the part of the lessee to erect any buildings. 

 14.               By way of Deed of Assignment dated 18 th February, 2022, the first appellant ("the appellant") acquired the interest of the respondents' former lessor in the head lease lands and the premises. In a letter to the respondents dated 13 th April, 2022, the appellant communicated his purchase of the leasehold interest as well as his intention to arrange an inspection of the premises to ascertain the respondents' compliance with various covenants. On 9 th May, 2022, the appellant served a Forfeiture Notice on the respondents, stating that he would seek forfeiture of the 1940 Lease on the basis of their alleged failure to keep the premises in " good and tenantable order, repair and condition " pursuant to Clause 7 of that lease. The respondents thereafter brought a successful application to restrain the appellant from re-entering the premises, and by High Court order dated 7 th November, 2022, O'Regan J. granted relief against forfeiture on certain conditions, the practical effect of which has been suspended pending the determination of this appeal. 

 15.               On 6 th May, 2022, the respondents sought by way of a Notice of Intention to acquire by purchase the fee simple and all intermediate interests in the property, pursuant to s. 4 of the 1967 Act. In a decision dated 13 th December, 2023, the County Registrar accepted, as a preliminary finding, that the 1940 Lease complied in all material respects with the requirements of the 1978 Act to purchase the fee simple, namely, the conditions of s. 9 and Conditions 1 and 7 of s. 10. The appellant's primary objection before the County Registrar rested on the contention that the absence of a building covenant in the 1893 Lease rendered that head lease a non-qualifying lease, thereby removing the sub-lessee's entitlement to acquire the fee simple in circumstances where the appellant was " not a person to whom [Part II of the 1978 Act] applies " under s. 16(2)(f). As the respondents failed to make an application within the period allowed for by ss. 16(2)(f)(i) and (ii) of the 1978 Act, the appellant submitted that their application was statute-barred. 

 16.               The County Registrar determined that interpreting the Ground Rents Legislation in this manner would serve to deny a whole cohort of leasehold owners the opportunity to secure the fee simple in their property in direct contravention of the purpose of that legislation. Having regard to the Law Reform Commission's 1998 Report, the County Registrar was satisfied that it was reasonable to interpret s. 16(2)(f) in light of the specific issue which that legislative reform sought to address, namely, a situation whereby a lessee without a qualifying lease granted a lease to a third party which would itself be a qualifying lease and enable that third party to acquire the fee simple in the property, particularly in the context of commercial supermarket developments. The respondents were accordingly entitled to acquire by purchase the fee simple interest and the County Registrar fixed the purchase price at 1,000, apportioned equally as between (a) the head leasehold interest held by the appellant and (b) the superior/freehold interest(s) of the holder(s) of which were unknown and unascertained. 

 17.               On appeal to the Circuit Court, the appellant sought an order to set aside the order of the County Registrar. The Circuit Court judge was satisfied that the 1940 Lease was a qualifying lease, having satisfied the conditions of s. 9 and Conditions 1 and 7 of s. 10. He found that the appellant had misconstrued the meaning and effect of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act, as he considered that the absence of a covenant to build in the head lease did not remove that lease from the scope of the 1978 Act. Further, the appellant failed to adduce any evidence to show that he, the head lessee, was not a person to whom the 1978 Act applied. The judge ultimately determined that the respondents' entitlement to acquire the fee simple interest was to be assessed by reference to the date of the grant of the 1940 Lease, as opposed to the date of the grant of the head lease. The Order of the Registrar was accordingly affirmed. 

 High Court Judgment ( [2024] IEHC 695 ) 

 18.               In a judgment dated 10 th December, 2024, Nolan J. refused the appellant's appeal and affirmed the order of the Circuit Court. With respect to the 1940 Lease, Nolan J. considered it " self-evident " that the respondents satisfied the requirements of s. 9 and one of the conditions in s. 10 of the 1978 Act (para. 27). Notably, no explicit finding was made by the High Court judge as to whether the 1893 Lease was a qualifying lease for the purposes of Part II of the 1978 Act; insofar as he proceeded to analyse the statutory purpose and interpretation of s. 16(2)(f), the judge appeared to implicitly accept that the Head Lease was non-qualifying. 

 19.               In the course of examining the parties' submissions on the interpretation and application of s. 16(2)(f), Nolan J. considered the appellant's reliance on the views expressed by Wylie in Landlord and Tenant Law (Bloomsbury Professional, 3 rd ed) at para 31.18, where the author purports to identify the " unintended consequences " of the introduction of s. 16(2)(f) and where, on one interpretation of the passage, it might be concluded that the existence of a building covenant in a head lease is a prerequisite to satisfying s. 16(2)(f): 

 " It applies only where the head lease contained a covenant to erect such buildings; many older leases will contain no such covenant nor any restriction on building, so that a sublessee may have erected such buildings quite lawfully yet be caught by the restriction and the new paragraph f. " 

 20.               Next, Nolan J. considered the respondents' reliance on the 1998 Report, in which the Law Reform Commission considered a potential misuse of the 1978 Act arising from the comments of Murphy J. in Wanze Properties (Ireland) Ltd v. Mastertron Ltd [1992] ILRM 746. In that case, Murphy J. accepted (albeit obiter ) that a lessee who did not hold under a qualifying lease could grant a lease to a third party which would itself be a qualifying lease to enable that third party to acquire the fee simple in the property. The Commission noted that this could have the effect of nullifying the intention of the superior landlord who had deliberately granted the lease in a particular form, believing that he was secure against any application to acquire the fee simple under the 1978 Act. In this context, the Commission invoked the example of a landowner of a shopping centre, whose intention to create a non-qualifying lease to a supermarket operator is defeated by the creation of qualifying subleases (see paras. 1.37 - 1.47 of the 1998 Report). The Commission accordingly recommended an amendment to the 1978 Act in the terms now expressed in ss. 16(2)(f) and 16(3) of the 1978 Act: 

 " We therefore recommend that a lessee who holds under a lease which is not a qualifying lease may not create a qualifying sub-lease, unless the only reason why the head-lease is not a qualifying lease is that the appropriate buildings have not yet been erected. " 

 21.               In light of the discussion in the 1998 Report and the decision in Wanze relied upon therein , Nolan J. considered it " abundantly clear " that the " mischief " intended to be addressed by s. 16(2)(f) was uniquely focused on the creation of leases surrounding the construction of supermarkets. In the absence of relevant case law regarding the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) and noting the " ambiguous and confusing " interaction of provisions within the 1978 Act, Nolan J. considered it appropriate to rely on s. 5(1)(b) of the Interpretation Act 2005 ("the 2005 Act") governing the construction of ambiguous or obscure provisions: 

 " 5.(1) In construing a provision of any Act (other than a provision that relates to the imposition of a penal or other sanction) 

 (a) that is obscure or ambiguous, or 

 (b) that on a literal interpretation would be absurd or would fail to reflect the plain intention of 

 (i) in the case of an Act to which paragraph (a) of the definition of "Act" in section 2 (1) relates, the Oireachtas, or 

 (ii) in the case of an Act to which paragraph (b) of that definition relates, the parliament concerned, 

 the provision shall be given a construction that reflects the plain intention of the Oireachtas or parliament concerned, as the case may be, where that intention can be ascertained from the Act as a whole." 

 22.               Nolan J. determined that the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) in the manner contended for by the appellant would constitute an " absurdity " which would fail to " reflect the plain intention of the Oireachtas " by disenfranchising the respondents and similarly situated tenants whose original lease did not contain a building covenant. This would have the effect of defeating the very purpose of the Ground Rents Legislation. The trial judge relied on Heather Hill Management Company CLG v. An Bord Pleanála and Others [2022] IESC 43 , [2024] 2 IR 222 in which Murray J. emphasised the importance of considering both the " immediate and approximate " context of an Act when interpreting its provisions. Having regard to the present " social conditions " in the context of " changing circumstances " (s. 6 of the 2005 Act), Nolan J. determined that "[t] he context is the purpose of purchasing the fee simple and the changing circumstance of those commercial developers which do not apply in this case " (para. 38). The respondent's lease could not, therefore, be construed as a non-qualifying lease within the meaning of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act. Nolan J. was satisfied that this interpretation was also proportionate and reflected the value that the parties have in the premises. 

 Determination 

 23.               The appellant was granted direct leave to appeal to this Court on 12 th May, 2025 ([2025] IESCDET 63). The Court determined this case to raise issues of general public importance as to the proper interpretation of s. 16(2)(f), insofar as the interpretation contended for by the appellant could have the effect of denying sub-lessees such as the respondents of their entitlement to acquire the fee simple, in respect of domestic dwellings that they or their predecessors-in-title would have built on foot of their sub-lease. The Attorney General was also invited to participate as a notice party to this appeal, in circumstances where issues surrounding the constitutional interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) could potentially arise. 

 Submissions 

 Is the Head Lease a Qualifying Lease? 

 24.               It is accepted by all parties that the respondents, as sub-lessees, are persons to whom Part II of the 1978 Act applies, with the High Court judge finding the ss. 9 and 10 requirements in respect of the 1940 Lease to be satisfied (para. 27). It is also acknowledged and accepted by all parties that, under s. 16(2)(f), the respondents are not entitled to acquire the fee simple in the premises unless the appellant himself is so entitled. In this regard, the respondents and Attorney General observe that the High Court did not make an explicit finding that the 1893 Lease is a non-qualifying lease; whether that is because it fails to satisfy the conditions under ss. 9 and 10 simpliciter , or because it does not contain a covenant to erect permanent buildings. The respondents and Attorney General submit that if the appellant is determined to be " a person to whom [Part II of the 1978 Act] applies ," the restriction in s. 16(2)(f) appears to have no application in the respondents' case. 

 25.               In his submissions, the appellant notes that the respondents have not cross-appealed from " the implicit finding " of the High Court that the Head Lease did not qualify under one of the alternative conditions in s. 10 and says that he will object to the introduction of this argument at the hearing of the appeal. For the sake of completeness, he addresses alternative Condition No. 1 in s. 10 and notes that the 1893 Lease identifies the head lease lands to include a house and outoffices, which, as a matter of necessary inference, were erected by the freehold owners. However, the appellant submits that the burden of proof ultimately rests with the respondents to prove the necessary facts to establish that the Head Lease is one to which Part II applies. Having failed to adduce that proof, the appellant submits that the High Court was entitled to find the Head Lease to be non-qualifying. Condition 2 is not substantively addressed by the appellant. The appellant maintains in the conclusion of his submissions that he has " no prospect of being able to acquire the fee simple interest " under Part II of the 1978 Act. 

 26.               The respondents submit that the appellant's original ground of opposition before the County Registrar - namely, that the respondents could not acquire the fee simple by virtue of the fact that the Head Lease was a non-qualifying lease due to the absence of a building covenant - gave rise to significant confusion as this argument was advanced before the Circuit Court and High Court. While the focus of the appellant's argument in the High Court concerned the narrow proposition relating to building covenants, the respondents contend that the appellant now seeks to put the issue in wider terms before this Court by focusing on a different question: " Does the sub-lessee have a right to acquire the fee simple where the Head Lessee does not?" 

 27.               The respondents ultimately contend that the appellant, as a holder of the lessee's interest under the 1893 Lease, is a person to whom Part II of the 1978 Act applies. It is submitted that the appellant satisfies the qualifying conditions in ss. 9 and 10 of the 1978 Act because (a) the head lease lands are held under a lease (the 1893 Lease); (b) the head lease lands are covered by permanent buildings and the unbuilt parts are subsidiary and ancillary; (c) there was no prohibition on buildings in the 1893 Lease; and (d) one, if not two of the seven alternative conditions in s. 10 of the 1978 Act have been satisfied: Condition 2 and, arguably, Condition 1: 

 " 1: that the permanent buildings or such of those permanent buildings as have caused the buildings to lose their original identity were erected by the person who at the time of their erection was entitled to the lessee's interest under the lease or were erected in pursuance of an agreement for the grant of the lease upon the erection of the permanent holdings ; 

 2:  that the lease is for a term of not less than fifty years and the yearly amount of the rent or the greatest rent reserved thereunder (whether redeemed at any time or not) is of an amount that is less than the amount of the rateable valuation of the property and that the permanent buildings on the land demised by the lease were not erected by the lessor or any superior lessor or any of their predecessors in title  ..." 

 28.               A number of conditions qualifying the operation of Condition 2 are then set out in that provision. The respondents contend that this Condition is satisfied, on the basis that the aggregate rateable valuation of the head lease lands exceeds the rent reserved by the 1893 Lease (while there are no valuation certificates in evidence to this effect, the respondents submit that it is open to the Court to make this inference given the sheer number of houses on the head lease lands), and there is no evidence to prove that the freehold owners built the head lease buildings. Further, it is suggested that Condition 1 may be satisfied, if that condition is understood to be met by the erection of permanent buildings by a sub-lessee on the basis that " the erection of a building by one's tenant is functionally indistinguishable from erecting it oneself [as head lessee]" (the Attorney appears to dispute this interpretation, on the basis that ss. 16(2)(c) and (3) appear to recognise the distinction between a lessee and sub-lessee). The respondents submit that if the evidence before this Court is considered insufficient to come to a conclusion on this matter, the appropriate step is to either permit the admission of new evidence regarding the rateable valuation of the head lease lands, or remit the matter to the County Registrar or High Court, in circumstances where the hearings in the lower courts focused on a much narrower question until now. They also submit that it is open to this Court to conclude that the appellant failed to discharge the burden of proof as the party relying on the restriction contained in s. 16(2)(f). 

 29.               The Attorney General agrees with the respondents' submissions and submits that, prima facie , the Head Lease is a qualifying lease under Part II of the 1978 Act. It is submitted that the High Court judge's judgment proceeded on the erroneous assumption that the head lease was not, in fact, a qualifying lease, in the absence of a covenant to build. 

 Statutory Interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act 

 30.               The appellant submits that the High Court judge erred in relying on the discussion in the 1998 Report when interpreting s. 16(2)(f) and consequently limiting the application of s. 16(2)(f) to either "large commercial developments" generally (judgment, para. 33), or supermarkets specifically (para. 30). The appellant argues that limiting the application of the section to these undefined terms introduces an " unworkably vague restriction " into the legislative scheme in the absence of an express reference to this effect. He contends that nowhere in the 1978 Act does the fee simple acquisition scheme distinguish between residential and commercial leases. It is noted that the LRC did not restrict its recommendations to commercial properties in its 1998 Report but chose to invoke the example of shopping centres to explain the difficulties presented by the 1978 Act, in light of the facts presented in Wanze. The appellant submits that distinguishing leases with reference to how later sub-leases are used will lead to arbitrary and unjust consequences. Ultimately, the appellant contends that the High Court's interpretation serves to amend the plain words of s. 16(2)(f) which have been intentionally enacted by the Oireachtas in those terms. 

 31.               Turning to the applicable rules of statutory interpretation, the appellant relies on a number of authorities in support of his contention that a literal construction of a provision is the primary, and most important consideration when interpreting a statute and cites the comments of Murray J. in Heather Hill , at para. 106, where he endorsed the statutory interpretation principles set out by McKechnie J. in DPP v. Brown [2018] IESC 67 , [2019] 2 IR 1 : " (i) The first and most important port of call is the words of the statute itself, those words being given their ordinary and natural meaning ...". With regard to the application of s. 5 of the 2005 Act, the appellant relies on Murray J.'s comments in Heather Hill to the effect that that section is engaged only where there is obscurity, ambiguity, absurdity, or a failure to reflect the plain intention of the Act when viewed as a whole (at para. 123). 

 32.               The appellant submits that the terms of s. 16(2)(f) are clear and unambiguous and, as such, do not give rise to an absurdity in the present case. The appellant argues that s. 16 clearly provides that a person shall not be entitled to acquire the fee simple under Part II if their landlord could not apply to acquire the fee simple interest themselves. The appellant maintains that as the appellant holds his lease " with no prospect of being able to acquire the fee simple ", the respondents do not meet the requisite criteria to avail of this limited statutory right. The appellant further submits that this Court should have regard to the presumption of constitutionality and double construction rule, which were applied in Shirley v. O'Gorman [2012] IESC 5 , [2012] 2 I.R. 170 in the context of interpreting s. 10(2) of the 1978 Act. In this respect, the appellant contends that this Court ought to interpret s. 16(2)(f) in a manner which protects his constitutionally protected property rights to the greatest degree possible and consider that restriction to capture both commercial and residential leases. 

 33.               The respondent's submissions do not expressly address the High Court's restrictive interpretation of s. 16(2)(f), but rather focus on the appellant's proposition that the absence of a covenant to build in a head lease renders that lease non-qualifying, such that a sub-lessee may not acquire the fee simple. The respondents submit that the appellant has failed to provide any linguistic or logical basis for this proposition, and contend that on a plain reading of Part II, s. 16(2)(f) does not operate to alter a head-lessee's qualifying criteria under ss. 9 and 10 by the addition of a new 'covenant to build' requirement. 

 34.               The respondents submit that the views expressed in Wylie which are relied upon by the appellant (and, it appears, by the High Court judge; cited at para. 20 above) to support this contention have, to a certain extent, been taken out of context. The respondents note that the relevant passage does not concern the operation of s. 16 but rather arises in the context of a discussion of Condition 7 of s. 10: a condition which can, but does not always, refer to leases which contain building covenants. That condition provides: - 

 " 7.  that the lease, being a lease for a term of not less than fifty years, was made 

 (a)    partly in consideration of the payment of a sum of money (other than rent) by the lessee to the lessor at or immediately before the grant of the lease and, for this purpose, any money paid in redemption of any part of the rent reserved by the lease (whether the money was paid in pursuance of a covenant in the lease or in pursuance of an agreement made between the lessee and the lessor during the currency of the lease) shall be deemed to be part of the consideration, or 

 (b)    partly in consideration of the expenditure (otherwise than on decoration) of a sum of money by the lessee on the premises demised by the lease, or 

 (c)    partly in consideration of both that payment and that expenditure, 

 where the sum so paid or expended or the total of those sums was not less than fifteen times the yearly amount of the rent or the greatest rent reserved by the lease, whichever is the less. " 

 35.               The respondents cite the passage relied upon by the appellant from the latest edition of Wylie (4 th ed, 2022) at para. 31.18: 

 "[The exception to the s. 16(2)(f) restriction set out in s. 16(3)] does not cover what is common in many older leases, that there is no covenant to build nor any restriction on building. Yet the sublessee may, quite lawfully, have erected permanent buildings but, as the provision in s. 76 [of the 2006 Act] is drafted, lost the right to acquire the fee simple unless a notice to acquire was served before 27 February 2006. This, probably unintended discrimination between sublessees must be of doubtful constitutionality " . 

 36.               The respondents comment that this passage is discussing the scope of the exclusion from the restriction contained in s. 16(3), not the operation of s. 16(2)(f) simpliciter . It is noted that this comment is made in the context of Condition 7 and does not suggest that a head lease which otherwise qualifies under a s. 10 alternative condition would cease to qualify because of anything in s. 16, or that the eligibility of a head lease under Part II is contingent on the existence of a building covenant therein. The respondents note that the author is rather highlighting the fact that the exclusion in s. 16(3) ought to have been enacted in wider terms and catch other situations where the actions of a sublessee might be attributed to the head lessee, so as to render the head lessee a qualifying person. In particular, the author suggests that such a situation may arise from a sub-lessee's satisfaction of Condition 1 in s. 10: if a sublessee erected permanent buildings, but a head-lessee did not, the head lease may not satisfy any of the s. 10 conditions and therefore leave the deserving sublessee with no remedy. 

 37.               The Attorney General agrees with the respondent that the High Court judgment was premised on the incorrect basis that the absence of a building covenant in the 1893 Lease rendered it non-qualifying. In this respect, the Attorney General also adopts the respondents' analysis of para 31.18 of Wylie, set out above. The Attorney nonetheless addresses the High Court judge's approach to statutory interpretation in construing s. 16(2)(f). He relies on the comments of Murray J. in Heather Hill to the effect that recourse should only be had to s. 5 of the 2005 Act where an ambiguity or obscurity in the provision is identified by reference to the " overall statutory context ", including " a consideration of the words in the section, the section when viewed in the light of the Act, the Act when viewed in the light of any relevant history, the well-established canons of construction and, if necessary, the purpose of the provision " (para. 123). In this respect, the Attorney General submits that it was unnecessary for the High Court judge to consider the provisions of s. 5 in circumstances where the intention of the Oireachtas can be clearly gleaned from a literal reading of s. 16(2)(f) in combination with s. 16(3); namely, that any sub-lessee is disqualified from acquiring the fee simple where the head-lessee does not so qualify. 

 38.               The Attorney submits that an interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) which purports to limit the application of that section to commercial premises appears to " fly in the face " of the specific wording of the s. 16(2)(f)(II) exception, in circumstances where that carve out for sub-lessees who made applications under Part III of 1978 Act before February 2006 would be unnecessary if s. 16(2)(f) did not apply equally to residential premises. Further, it is submitted that the " mischief " identified by the Law Reform Commission in the context of shopping centres and supermarket operators applies with equal force to residential properties; for example, if a lessee in a block of flats granted a qualifying sub-lease to a third party, they could frustrate the restriction set out in s. 16(2)(a) of the 1978 Act and relieve the flat owner of the covenants necessary for the proper management of the apartment complex. 

 Constitutionality of s. 16(2)(f) 

 39.               Neither the appellant nor the respondent have challenged the constitutionality of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act. The appellant submits that insofar as the Attorney General makes submissions directed towards a constitutional reading of that section, he reserves the right to address those submissions at the hearing of this appeal. The respondents acknowledge that while a determination of unconstitutionality would assist them, they can nonetheless succeed without such a ruling (as, on their submissions, the head lease is a qualifying one to which Part II applies). 

 40.               In these circumstances, the Attorney General submits that it is not necessary for this Court to make a determination on the constitutional validity of s. 16(2)(f). It is noted that this Court is not permitted to give " gratuitous advice on legal issues to the Oireachtas and the Government, a function which was never conferred on it by the Constitution " ( Salaja v Minister for Justice, Equality and Law Reform [2011] IEHC 51 para. 7; Lofinmakin v Minister for Justice [2013] IESC 49 , [2013] 4 IR 274 , 291). Further, the constitutionality of s. 16(2)(f) was not raised in the High Court (see Blehein v Murphy [2000] 2 IR 231 at 240). 

 41.               Should this Court deem it necessary to rule on this issue, the Attorney affirms the constitutionality of s. 16(2)(f) for a number of reasons. It is noted that neither of the parties have sought to adduce evidence to rebut the presumption of constitutionality which applies to that section. While accepting that the expropriation or divestment of private property rights without compensation will usually be considered unconstitutional in the absence of exceptional circumstances (citing inter alia, ESB v. Good & Ors [2025] IESC 27 ), it is submitted that s. 16(2)(f) does not abrogate or constitute an " unjust attack " on the property rights of certain lessees under Articles 40.3 or 43. Rather, s. 16(2)(f) was enacted to correct the lacuna in the 1978 Act and remedy a situation whereby a person could " artificially create " property rights, which they would not otherwise have. Insofar as it might be considered that the amendment contravenes property rights by operating retrospectively, the Attorney submits that s. 16(2)(f)(ii) provides an appropriate carve out for sub-lessees of non-qualifying head lessees who applied to acquire the fee simple before 27 th February 2006. In this respect, the "right" to acquire the fee simple only crystallises when it is invoked by either service of a notice of intention to acquire the fee simple (s. 4 of the 1967 Act) or application to the Registrar of Titles (ss. 20 and 21 of the 1978 Act). Any person who actually invoked their right to acquire the fee simple based on the law as it stood before 27 th February 2006 is therefore protected. The Attorney concludes that there is significant public interest in ensuring that the property rights are not artificially created and landlords consequently disenfranchised. 

 The Conduct of the proceedings 

 42.               In order to understand the issues that arise for consideration in this appeal, it is important to look in the first instance at the history of these proceedings. These proceedings commenced with the notice of application to acquire the fee simple of the premises concerned issued on the 12 th April, 2023. The matter came before the County Registrar for Cork who gave a written decision on the application on the 13 th December, 2023. In the course of her decision, the County Registrar observed that the effect of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act was the issue to be decided. She noted that it was not contentious that the 1940 lease under which the respondents held their title satisfied the provisions of s. 9 and s. 10(1)(vii) of the 1978 Act. She dealt with a number of ancillary points which are of no relevance here. She then considered the principal objection of the appellant to the entitlement of the respondent to acquire the fee simple based on the provisions of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act. It was argued before her that the absence of a covenant to build in the head lease rendered the head lease a non-qualifying lease under s. 16(2)(f). In those circumstances, it was contended that, as the respondents had not made the application to buy out the fee simple prior to the 27 th February, 2006, as provided for in s. 16(2)(f), the application was statute barred. The County Registrar rejected the arguments of the appellant saying: 

 "At its most basic, the ground rents legislation came into being to address the reality left over from English occupation, such that ordinary citizens of the State could secure the fee simple interest in their property, fee simple ownership being preferred by the modern Irish State over the prevalent English landlord. It is agreed by the parties that, but for any potentially negative interpretation of s.16(2)(f), the lease is a qualifying lease in the ordinary course prior to 2006. 

 If I interpret section 16(2)(f) as argued by the First Named [appellant] , I am denying a whole cohort of leasehold owners the opportunity to secure the fee simple in their property in direct contravention of the very purpose of the legislation. 

 I find the Law Reform Commission report on Land Law and Conveyancing Law (LRC 56/1998) to be of assistance, in that it explains what potential problem was envisaged that section 16(2)(f) was intended to solve. (Namely, the very narrow situation where a lessee without a qualifying lease could grant a lease to a third party, which would itself be a qualifying lease, referencing particular issues pertaining to commercial leases in shopping centres). I am satisfied that it is reasonable for me to interpret that section in light of the specific issue (that does not arise in this particular case) identified in the Law Reform Commission Report. To do otherwise would, to use the First Named [appellant's] own phrase "constitute an impermissible collateral attack upon" the very purpose of the Landlord And Tenant (Ground Rents) (No. 2) Act, 1978. Wylie writes in Irish Landlord and Tenant Law, submitted by the First Named [appellant] , "it is not uncommon that a lease may not contain a covenant to build. To follow the first [appellant's] argument would serve to greatly alter the entitlement of lessees under the legislation" 

      Accordingly, an order was made permitting the respondents herein to buy out the fee simple. 

 43.               The decision of the County Registrar was then appealed to the Circuit Court. It was recorded in the decision of the court (Judge O'Donohue) that the appeal was based on the ground that the respondents were not entitled to acquire the fee simple by virtue of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act. It was put thus by Judge O'Donoghue: 

 "Simply put the first named [appellant] argues that as there is no covenant in the head lease to build and no restriction on building, accordingly there is no entitlement, and the [respondent] is a non-qualifying person." 

 44.               As was noted by the Circuit Court, it was necessary for the respondents to establish that they satisfy the requirements of s. 9, and one of the conditions set out in s. 10 of the 1978 Act, in order to acquire the fee simple. The court was satisfied that the respondent satisfied the requirements of s. 9 and s. 10(1)(vii) of the 1978 Act. As to the arguments of the appellant, the Circuit Court judge concluded that the appellant had misconstrued the meaning and effect of s. 16(2)(f), saying as follows: 

 "The absence of building covenants in a head lease does not mean that the head lease is a lease to which the Ground Rent Acts do not apply. The [respondent] submits that this is a question to be assessed at the date of the grant of the lease, not the date of the grant of the head lease.  The absence of such a covenant, in the opinion of the court, does not equate to an absence of an entitlement to acquire the fee simple under the 1978 Act. There has been no evidence adduced by the first named [appellant] to show that the head lessee was not a person to whom the Act applied." 

 45.               The decision of the Circuit Court was then appealed to the High Court. I have already set out in some detail the terms of the judgment of Nolan J. It is interesting to note the submissions of the appellant furnished to the High Court following the oral hearing of the case.  In those submissions, the appellant observed that the issues in the case distilled down to one simple question; 

 "Does a sub-lessee have a right to acquire the fee simple where the head lessee does not?"  

 46.               The appellant went on to say: 

 "It is accepted, as it was at the oral hearing, that the [respondents] do have a qualifying lease subject only to the restriction in s.16(2)(f). If that restriction applies in the present case, the [appellant] argues then the [respondents] do not have the right to acquire the fee simple." 

 47.               Ultimately, as we have seen, the judgment of the High Court rejected the arguments of the appellant and concluded that the contention of the appellant as to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) was not correct. The judge was of the view that the Oireachtas, in enacting the provisions of this section, intended: 

 48.               " [T] o prohibit a lessee who did not hold under a qualifying lease, granting a lease to a third party which would become a qualifying lease, to enable a third party to acquire the fee simple to the property in the context of large commercial developments. It was not intended to exclude or disenfranchise the [respondents] or the many similar tenants who live on the Huggartsland lands and indeed the many other tenants which Mr. Wylie refers to, whose original lease did not contain a building covenant (para. 33)The matter was then appealed to this Court. Once more, the appellant, in the written submissions before the Court identified the principal issue before the Court as being: 

 "Can a sub-lessee, who otherwise qualifies for relief under the 1978 Act, acquire a fee simple interest in lands where a superior lessee could not?" 

 49.               Although the wording set out in the submissions referred to above may be marginally different to those contained in the appellant's High Court submissions, the gist of the question remains the same. 

 50.               The submissions of the appellants and the respondents, together with those of the Attorney General, have been described in some detail above, and it is not necessary to set out the details of those submissions again. However, it may be helpful to mention briefly the responses of the parties to a request for clarification which was sent to them prior to the hearing of the appeal. The first question raised by the Court concerned the reasons behind the enactment of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act, and whether it was intended to deal with the consequences of the decision in Wanze and was thus concerned with issues relating to the construction of supermarkets and/or commercial developments. The response from the appellant and from the respondents to this question was broadly similar. The appellant accepted that it was intended to deal with a potential issue first identified in Wanze , but added that there was nothing in the legislative language, nor in the Law Reform Commission's report, which inspired it, to suggest that the amendment was intended to be restricted to commercial developments and/or supermarkets. Likewise, the respondents accepted that the enactment was motivated by the circumstances identified in Wanze and following on from the decision expressed in the recommendation of the Law Reform Commission, and it was further accepted by the respondents that the motivation for the amendment and the recommendation of the Law Reform Commission did not limit the application of the enactment to cases involving particular types of permanent buildings or to permanent buildings used for particular purposes. Accordingly, both the appellant and the respondent rejected the interpretation placed on the provisions of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act, to the effect that the intention of the Oireachtas in legislating in those terms was to deal with the situation that could arise in relation to non-qualifying lessees to enable a third party to acquire the fee simple in the context of large commercial developments as found by the High Court.  (See para. 33 of the judgment of the High Court). The position of the Attorney General was somewhat similar. It was also accepted in the response by the Attorney General that the enactment of s. 16(2)(f) was not confined to the consequences of the decision in Wanze only. As expressed by the Attorney General, it was said that its purpose was " to deal with the problem more broadly of a non-qualifying lessee granting a qualifying lease to a sub-lessee, thereby entitling the sub-lessee to acquire the fee simple and any immediate interest in a manner which was not envisaged by the Act, and in what was in breach of the principle of property law that a tenant cannot have a better title than his landlord ". Thus, it was pointed out that the problem identified in the section was one that applied equally to commercial and residential premises. 

 51.               It is undoubtedly the case that it was the respondents who had contended for that argument, and had successfully persuaded the High Court judge to reach the conclusion that the Oireachtas had intended the amendment introduced by s. 16(2)(f) to apply to commercial properties only. Thus, the response of the respondents to that question was a significant departure from the arguments previously relied on by them. 

 52.               The second question raised was as follows: 

 "Is it contended by the appellant that a lease which does not contain a covenant to erect permanent buildings cannot be a lease to which Part II of the 1978 Act applies?"

In other words, a principal part of the case originally made by the appellant was conceded. It was pointed out that the absence of a building covenant is principally relevant to s. 10, Condition 7, and to s. 16(3) of the 1978 Act and, so far as this was concerned, it was pointed out that there was no disagreement between the appellant and the respondents. The appellant went on to add the following observation:

 56.               For completeness, it should be noted that the Attorney General also took the approach of not responding to this question, given that it was a question directed to the appellant.

To be captured, it would have to be a non-qualifying lease. Were it not for such a finding, the High Court would not have had any need to consider the consequences of the arguments in relation to the correct interpretation of s. 16(2)(f).

 "The issue identified in the High Court judgment presents as a binary dispute, between two competing contentions, namely:
