 62.               Finally, in this context, it should be noted that, once again, the question concerned being primarily addressed to the appellant, the Attorney General did not furnish any response to that question. 

 The Hearing before this Court 

 63.               When the appeal commenced before this Court, counsel on behalf of the appellant noted that the issue relied on by the respondents as to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) had fallen away, in that the respondents did not seek to stand over the High Court interpretation of the section, to the effect that, in enacting s. 16(2)(f), it was intended by the Oireachtas that those provisions would apply only to supermarket/commercial leases. Rather, it was said that the parties were in agreement that the terms of s. 16(2)(f) applied to leases generally. Obviously, there could have been no disagreement on that point, given the response by the respondents to the request for clarification from the Court. 

 64.               Counsel for the appellant then argued that, in those circumstances, the head lease was a non-qualifying lease, in circumstances where there had never been any evidence led to support the argument that the head lease was one to which Part II of the 1978 Act applied.  Accordingly, the underlying argument being made was that in those circumstances the appeal must succeed, and the respondents must fail in their application to buy out the ground rent. In other words, the appellant was no longer relying on the key argument that had been made throughout the proceedings, that unless there was a covenant to build in the head lease, it was a non-qualifying lease and the respondents could not acquire the fee simple. That was always the case made by the appellant but now, the appellant seeks to make a different case, namely that the respondents had failed to prove that the head lease was a qualifying lease such that the appellant as head lessee was entitled to buy out the fee simple. 

 65.               It is unfortunate to say the least that in the circumstances of this case this Court found itself dealing with an appeal on a point that had found favour with the High Court in relation to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) and the argument that it applied to commercial leases only and then for the party that had urged that point on the High Court to abandon it following the grant of leave to appeal to this Court. It is even more unfortunate that the party who had succeeded in obtaining leave to appeal on the interpretation of the section should also have abandoned the core argument of their case which had been made at every hearing between the parties, namely that for the fee simple to be acquired it was necessary that the head lease contained a building covenant.  

 66.               Before dealing with the problem thrown up by this unusual set of circumstances, it may be helpful to make a few brief observations on the points raised by the parties and now abandoned. To take the issue of s. 16(2)(f), it is not in dispute that the amendment to the 1978 Act by which s. 16(2)(f) was inserted resulted from the decision in Wanze followed by the recommendation of the Law Reform Commission. It was introduced to prevent what was seen as a problem in relation to commercial leases which could give rise to an entitlement to buy out the fee simple contrary to the landowner's intentions. The problem identified by the Law Reform Commission was described in detail at paras 1.37 to 1.47 in the 1998 Report. The focus of the recommendation was on leases of supermarkets and other commercial premises. It is not surprising then, that when it came to a consideration of the section, that it was thought to relate to commercial/supermarket premises. However, it is clear that no language was used in the section that could have resulted in such a restricted meaning of the section. It was only by reference to the history behind the introduction of the section that it could possibly have been understood to have been so restricted. After all, the section was introduced following the recommendation of the Law Reform Commission to deal with the problem identified in Wanze. Nevertheless, the words used in s. 16(2)(f) contain no limitation as to their application and on a literal construction of the words used do not bear a construction limiting its effect to commercial/supermarket premises only.  Accordingly, it was correct for the respondents to abandon their argument on this point. It is therefore accepted by the respondents that if the lease on foot of which it is sought to rely to buy out the ground rent is a sublease, it will not be a qualifying lease unless the head lease is also a qualifying lease. 

 67.               The argument of the appellant to the effect that the head lease had to contain a building covenant was misconceived. There is nothing in the ground rents legislation to support such a contention. A lease can be a building lease which requires the lessee to build but that is not a necessary requirement under the legislation. A lease which neither requires the lessee to build and does not restrict the lessee from building is all that is required. As it was put by the respondents, "... the absence of a covenant to build does not equate to an absence of an entitlement to acquire the fee simple under the Ground Rent Acts. The absence of such a covenant is in no way conclusive as to the existence of such an entitlement ." I agree with that submission and therefore it was appropriate for the appellant to abandon this point notwithstanding that it had been the sole plank of his objection to the entitlement of the respondents to acquire the fee simple throughout the proceedings. 

 68.               Where does that leave this appeal? The basis upon which leave was granted has now disappeared from the case and the appellant seeks to rely on a new ground which was not the subject of argument previously. Essentially, counsel for the appellant sought to argue that as the point raised by the respondents as to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) had been abandoned, it was necessary for them to establish the head lease was a qualifying lease and it was argued that at no stage throughout the proceedings to date had they done so. There was no evidence provided before any of the hearings to date to deal with that issue and therefore, in the absence of any application to adduce such evidence, the proceedings should be finalised by setting aside the order permitting them to buy out the fee simple. It was further said that as the ultimate owner of the head lease had not been ascertained, their interest should have been considered by the County Registrar, the Circuit Court and the High Court, each of which had an obligation to ensure that each element of the test for acquiring a fee simple had been complied with. This was also a point which had not been made previously. 

 69.               Counsel for the respondents in their submissions noted that a number of issues were now agreed. It is agreed that in order to buy out the fee simple, the applicant has to show that the lease under which he holds his interest is compliant with s. 9 and one of the conditions of s. 10 of the 1978 Act. It is not disputed that the respondents are,  prima facie , entitled to buy out the fee simple herein as they comply with the requirements of s. 9 and s. 10 of the 1978 Act. There is no dispute as to the interpretation of s. 16 (2)(f) and it cannot be limited in its application to leases of commercial/supermarket premises. It is also agreed that a building covenant in a lease is not a prerequisite for the acquisition of the fee simple interest under the provisions of ss. 9, 10 and 16 of the 1978 Act. It is in relation to the application of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act in this case that the parties diverge. 

 70.               Section 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act, as has been seen, restricts the right to acquire the fee simple. Thus, it provides that a person shall not be entitled to acquire the fee simple if the lease on which such right is based is a sublease of land granted by a lessee who is not a person to whom Part II of the Act applies. Certain exceptions to this general provision are then set out but they are not relevant on the facts of this case. What is not in dispute here is that the respondents are sub-lessees. On the face of it, it would appear, therefore, that to acquire the fee simple, it must be established that the head lease was one which would have enabled the lessee under the head lease to acquire the fee simple. 

 71.               The proposition stated above gives rise to a number of issues arising in part from the somewhat unsatisfactory manner in which this case has been presented.  I will return to these issues subsequently. 

 72.               It will be recalled that when leave to appeal in this matter was granted it was considered that an issue could arise as to the proper constitutional interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act. Accordingly, the Attorney General was provided with a copy of the Determination and invited to participate in the appeal, if that was considered appropriate. The Attorney General was satisfied that it was appropriate to participate in the appeal, and accordingly provided written submissions with counsel appearing in court on behalf of the Attorney General. As was observed by counsel on behalf of the Attorney General, given that a number of issues between the parties as to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) were resolved in the course of the hearing, counsel was not obliged to address the arguments put forward by the appellant and the respondent in relation to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f). In his submissions to the Court, counsel for the Attorney General made reference to the provisions of the Landlord and Tenant (Ground Rents) Act, 1967 and, in particular, to s. 3(3) of that Act. It noted that similar restrictions to those contained in ss. 9 and 10 of the 1978 Act similarly applied. It was pointed out that an unsuccessful lessee precluded by the provisions of s. 16(2)(f) from acquiring the fee simple was nevertheless left with an entitlement to a reversionary lease, subject to paying an annual rent. 

 73.               The point was made that ss. 9 and 10 of the 1978 Act, as amended, simply set out the terms which have to be complied with in order to acquire the fee simple. The point was emphasised that the provisions of s. 16 of the Act did not apply Part II of the 1978 Act, but qualified the entitlement to acquire the fee simple. Accordingly, it was agreed by counsel on behalf of the Attorney General that the position under the provisions of ss. 9 and 10, together with s. 16(2)(f), is that if the head lessee did not qualify to acquire the fee simple, the sub-lessee was precluded from acquiring the fee simple. 

 The Ultimate Disposition of this Case 

 74.               It is most unusual for an appeal to this Court to undergo such fundamental change since its arrival in this Court. The case started off with an argument that the sub-lessee could not acquire the fee simple unless the head lease contained a covenant to build. That argument was relied on before the County Registrar and was finally abandoned in this Court. The argument of the respondents maintained that s. 16(2)(f) of the 1978 Act, which might otherwise preclude them from acquiring the fee simple, had to be interpreted as applying only to commercial/supermarket premises having regard to the background to its introduction. That argument was also abandoned in this Court. Where does this approach now leave these proceedings? 

 75.               In this context, it would perhaps be useful to remind ourselves of the provisions of s. 9 of the 1978 Act which are set out above. Thus, Part II of the 1978 Act applies to a person who holds land under a lease, provided a number of conditions are complied with, namely, that there are permanent buildings on the land, and that the portion of the land not covered by those buildings is subsidiary and ancillary to them. Other conditions relate to the situation where an alteration or a reconstruction of the permanent buildings has taken place, and a provision to the effect that the permanent buildings or, if applicable, any alteration or reconstruction were not erected in contravention of the covenant in the lease. Finally, s. 9 requires that, in order to acquire the fee simple, not only must those conditions be met but also one of the alternative conditions set out in s. 10 must also be met. 

 76.               Section 10 contains a number of additional conditions and, as has been seen from s. 9, only one of those needs to be applicable in order for the lessee to acquire the fee simple. I will set out only three of the conditions as they are the three conditions relied on by the respondents herein, namely: 

 "(i)      that the permanent buildings, or such of those permanent buildings as have caused the buildings to lose their original identity, were erected by the person who at the time of their erection was entitled to the lessee's interest under the lease, or were erected in pursuance of an agreement for the grant of the lease upon the erection of the permanent buildings. 

 (ii)        that the lease is for a term of not less than 50 years and the yearly amount of the rent or the greatest rent reserved thereunder (whether redeemed at any time or not) is of an amount that is less than the amount of the rateable valuation of the property at the date of service under section 4 of the Act of 1967, of notice of intention to acquire the fee simple, or the date of an application under Part III of this Act, as the case may be, and that the permanent buildings on the land demised by the lease were not erected by the lessor, or any superior lessor, or any of their predecessors in title: provided that it shall be presumed, until the contrary is proved, that the buildings were not so erected. 

 (iii)       that the lease, being a lease for a term of not less than 50 years, was made: 

 (a)        partly in consideration of the payment of a sum of money (other than rent) by the lessee to the lessor at. or immediately before the grant of the lease, and, for this purpose, any money paid in redemption of any part of the rent reserved by the lease (whether the money was paid in pursuance of a covenant in the lease, or in pursuance of an agreement made between the lessee and the lessor during the currency of the lease) shall be deemed to be part of the consideration, or 

 (b)        partly in consideration of the expenditure (otherwise than on decoration) of a sum of money by the lessee on the premises demised by the lease, or 

 (c)        partly in consideration of both that payment and that expenditure, 

 where the sum so paid or expended, or the total of those sums, was not less than 15 times the yearly amount of the rent, or the greatest rent reserved by the lease, whichever is the less." 

 77.               Leaving aside the question of the burden of proof, the argument was made by the appellant that it was necessary for the respondents, in respect of s. 10, Condition 1, to establish that, in circumstances where the head lease in this case identifies that in 1893 the lands demised by the Cramers included a " house and outoffices " to establish who erected the buildings on the land. It was said that there was a necessary inference that those buildings were erected by the freehold owners given the terms of the demise. As a result, it was said that it was then a question as to whether those buildings have lost their original identity through the erection of other buildings or works by the appellant. It was pointed out that there was no evidence before the Circuit Court or the High Court to deal with that issue. It was in those circumstances that it is argued by the appellant that it was a matter for the respondents to prove that the head lease was a qualifying lease before they could acquire the fee simple in the property, and having failed to adduce that proof, the High Court was entitled to proceed, as it did, to consider the meaning of s. 16(2)(f). The respondents, not surprisingly, take issue with this assertion on the part of the appellant. For my part, I am inclined to agree with the respondents. It seems to me to be reasonable to take the view that the High Court judge came to a conclusion on the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) on the basis that he was satisfied that, if that provision applied to the respondents, then they were not entitled to buy out the fee simple.  However, I am far from convinced that he came to that view because he was not satisfied that the respondents had satisfied the necessary requirements of s. 10, Condition 1. Rather, the trial judge was focused on the absence of a covenant to build. See, in particular, the discussion at paras. 17 to 19 of the judgment of the High Court. Having considered the arguments of the appellant, to the effect that the head lease did not contain a covenant to build, he observed: 

 "A large number of homes similar to this premises and the one owned by the Respondent, were built on the lands which has become a well-known area in the city of Cork. If this submission were correct, no sub tenant would ever be able to purchase the fee simple, notwithstanding that may affect hundreds of perspective purchasers." 

 78.               In other words, the trial judge's mind was, at all times, addressed to the question of whether or not there was a covenant to build contained in the head lease, and he was focused on that, and was not, as such, focused on any specific condition set out in s. 10.  Thus, I feel that it would be wrong to approach this issue on the basis that, because the High Court judge was not satisfied that the respondents had not shown that they came within any of the conditions set out in s. 10, that he proceeded to consider the requirements of s. 16(2)(f). 

 79.               It is fair to say that, following the hearing before the High Court, written submissions were furnished by both parties to the High Court, in which it was said that the head lease could not qualify under s. 10, Condition 1, in circumstances where the buildings on the land were erected by the sub-lessee and not the head lessee and, therefore, it was pointed out that s. 10(1) could not apply in the circumstances of this case. The respondents in their written submissions simply did not address that point, presumably because of the timing of that submission having been made. The position, therefore, is that the issue as to whether or not the head lessee would have satisfied the conditions set out in s. 9, together with any one of the conditions in s. 10, simply has not been addressed at any stage of the proceedings to date. 

 80.               There was a discussion in the course of the hearing as to whether or not it was an obligation on the part of the person seeking to buy out the fee simple to show that they were not precluded from doing so by reason of the provisions of s. 16(2)(f). Leaving aside the question of whether it was a necessary proof for an applicant to establish that s. 16(2)(f) did not apply, or whether it was necessary for the owner of the fee simple to raise the application of the section by way of objection to the entitlement to buy out the fee simple, the way in which this case was dealt with meant that no evidence was adduced by either side to deal with the matters set out in s. 10 of the 1978 Act in respect of the position of the head lessee and his entitlement to acquire the fee simple. 

 81.               Whatever the position as to who was responsible for raising the issue of whether the head lessee came within the conditions, or one of them set out in s. 10, it is beyond dispute that the only point raised by the appellant was the absence of a building covenant in the head lease, and that the respondents simply did not engage with the application of s. 10 to the head lessee at all. However, the respondents have now sought to engage to some extent with these issues in their submissions to this Court. Further, the submission was made by the respondents that there were a number of approaches that could be taken by this Court at this stage in order to reach a conclusion on this appeal. The first suggestion made was that it was open to the Court to infer that the rateable valuation for the purpose of Condition 2 of s. 10 exceeds the rent reserved by the 1893 lease. Alternatively, it was suggested that, given that s. 16(2)(f) was raised as a defence by the appellant in the hearing of the application to acquire the fee simple, it was open to this Court to conclude that the appellant had failed to discharge the burden of proof as the party relying on that restriction. 

 82.               Further, it was suggested that it was open to the Court to admit new evidence in the form of a certificate in respect of the rateable valuation of the lands involved in the head lease. In the absence of obtaining such a valuation, it was suggested that it would be open to the Court to admit new evidence of a secondary nature as to the rateable valuation from a chartered surveyor. The reason for that proposition was because of the length of time that can be required in order to obtain a certificate of rateable valuation. 

 83.               The final alternative proposed was that this Court should remit the matter to the appropriate court so that the question of rateable valuation, and any other issues relating to the eligibility of the 1893 lease, could be addressed. 

 84.               It should be said that, in the course of their submissions, the respondents focused primarily on Condition 2 of s. 10, which relates to the rateable valuation, and I will come back to that in a moment. However, in respect of Condition 1 of s. 10, an argument was made on behalf of the respondents that, contrary to the views expressed by Wylie, and referred to previously, that the erection of a building by one's tenant is functionally indistinguishable from erecting it oneself. It was suggested that the word " by " in Condition 1 cannot be interpreted so literally as to mean that the head lessee or sub-lessee has physically done the work. It was suggested that, if the head lessee puts in place a contract, that is to say a sublease whereby for good consideration a building is erected on the lands concerned, he or she has invested no less in the land than a lessee who pays a builder to do so. Whilst acknowledging that that construction of Condition 1 would entail, in the context of the lease and sub-lease, a conclusion that both the head lessee and sub-lessee have performed the same task, it nevertheless is argued that this resolves an anomaly in the legislation. It was this anomaly that led Wylie to the view that " discrimination between sub-lessees must be of doubtful constitutionality ." 

 85.               It should also be said that the appellant did not engage fully with the respondents attempt to interpret s. 10, Condition 1, in this manner. For my part, I would be very reluctant to go down the route of interpreting s. 10, Condition 1, in the manner suggested by the respondents, without the benefit of a full argument as to its proper interpretation. On the face of it, the situation of a sub-lease in this case appears to be that which is intended to be caught by the terms of s. 16(2)(f), as highlighted by the concern expressed by Wylie in the passage referred to above. Accordingly, I would not infer in this case that the respondents could succeed by relying on the provisions of s. 10, Condition 1 without a full argument as to the interpretation of that clause. 

 86.               That brings me to a consideration of whether or not the respondents can rely on s. 10, Condition 2.  Essentially, in regard to Condition 2, it is necessary to establish that the yearly amount of the rent, that is to say the ground rent, is less than the amount of the rateable valuation of the property.  It is, of course, the case that no evidence was adduced by either side in relation to the rateable valuation of the property. 

 87.               The rent reserved under the head lease was the sum of £16, 10s, or 20.95. There is no certificate of rateable valuation. It is also apparent that a significant number of houses have now been built on the lands comprised in the head lease. There is a real possibility that the amount of the rateable valuation is greater than the amount of the rent reserved. However, the question for this Court is whether it is appropriate to proceed to draw an inference as to compliance with s. 10, Condition 2, or whether the matter should be remitted to the High Court to enable evidence of the rateable valuation to be formally provided. 

 88.               Counsel on behalf of the appellant has submitted that s. 10, Condition 2, by defining in para. c what is meant by " rateable valuation ", mandates that a formal certificate must be provided by the Commissioner of Valuation in relation to the property. As mentioned previously, it is the respondents' case that the Court can infer the amount of the rateable valuation without the necessity to obtain a certificate, but that, if the Court takes the view that a certificate is necessary, then the appropriate thing to do is to allow the matter to proceed by obtaining such evidence. That may be by remitting the matter to the High Court or, no doubt, by adjourning this case to enable the certificate to be obtained. It goes without saying that, as a matter of practice, when a party seeks to rely on s. 10, Condition 2, for the purpose of acquiring the fee simple, then the best evidence in relation to rateable valuation is the certificate of valuation and, therefore, such certificate ought to be provided, if possible, in order to satisfy the requirements of s. 10, Condition 2. 

 89.               Counsel on behalf of the appellant has argued that, in circumstances where the respondents have simply failed to adduce one of the necessary proofs in relation to their entitlement to acquire the fee simple and where the respondents effectively abandoned their opposition to the appeal by reference to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f), this  should result in the appeal being granted simpliciter , and the orders of the High Court, Circuit Court and County Registrar should be set aside. Counsel for the respondents pointed out that the normal practice in relation to ground rent applications is that, in circumstances where a party has omitted to produce an essential proof, time will usually be granted to enable that to be done.  As was said, this is not typical litigation inter partes  where there is a winner and loser, but rather it is a situation in which one party is invoking a right and, accordingly, if there is a failure of proof, there is nothing to prevent a party from coming back again once their proofs are in order. 

 Final Observations 

 90.               There are a few observations which may be useful to make at this particular point.  While the parties have made submissions to  this Court as to how this case should now be disposed of by the Court, it would, perhaps be wise to step back for a moment to reconsider how this case started off before the County Registrar and ultimately came to be before this Court. This case started off as a straight-forward application to buy out a ground rent. The appellant was, of course, entitled to object to the respondent's entitlement to do so by reference to the argument as to the requirement of a building covenant in the head lease.  Having lost before the County Registrar, the appellant appealed and that point was again the subject of argument before the Circuit Court. Having failed in the Circuit Court, the appellant then appealed to the High Court. On each occasion, the appeal was brought by the appellant in relation to the finding as to whether there was a requirement for a building covenant in the head lease. That was the argument made throughout the proceedings as to why the respondents were not entitled to buy out the fee simple. It framed the basis on which this Court granted leave to appeal.  Yet it is now finally (and only before this Court at the last minute and in response to specific questions by the Court) accepted on behalf of the appellant that this argument was wrong and misconceived. 

 91.               The hearing before the High Court was not helped by the arguments of the respondents in relation to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f), an argument which succeeded before the High Court and which is now accepted by the respondents to be wrong - albeit prompted by a wholly incorrect construction of the legislation advanced by the appellant  as to the requirement for a building covenant in the head lease. Nevertheless, as was pointed out in the course of the hearing this is a case in which leave to appeal was given to the appellant on the basis that a matter of general public importance arose in respect of the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f). Having granted leave to appeal, the appellant sought to conduct the appeal before this Court on an entirely different basis to that upon which leave was granted, namely, whether or not the head lease was a qualifying lease under s. 10, or any of its conditions.  The respondents then sought to place reliance principally on Condition 2 relating to the rateable valuation. None of the earlier judgments and orders in these proceedings touched on the question of whether the requirements of s. 10 had been met because the case was always run by the appellant on the basis that the respondents could never comply with the provisions of s. 16(2)(f) in the absence of a building covenant in the head lease. If this case had not taken off down a cul-de-sac, no doubt, at some stage, the necessity to establish the rateable valuation of the property comprised in the head lease would have arisen. Indeed, an issue may have arisen as to whether the requirement was to establish the rateable valuation of the head lease as a whole, or only an apportionment of the rateable valuation relating to this specific property. 

 92.               What is, undoubtedly, the case is that this Court cannot take the course suggested by the appellant, namely, that, in circumstances where the arguments in respect of the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) have fallen away, that the appeal should be allowed and the orders of the courts below should be set aside with no further orders. To do that would be extremely unfair to the respondents given that at all times they had attempted to deal with the arguments actually put forward by the appellant. This would mean that a party who had pursued one line or argument throughout the conduct of the proceedings could, by taking an entirely different line of argument in this Court  achieve a successful outcome. That could never be an appropriate way to conduct litigation. In practical terms, a party, be it an applicant or a respondent is supposed to engage with the facts and the circumstances of the particular case, and to ensure that any points they wish to rely on are made before the court in an appropriate way so that there is a considered decision provided by the relevant court having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and any issues of law arising on those facts. In this case, it is quite clear that all of the decisions made at the various stages in these proceedings were made on a consideration of the arguments that had been made before the respective courts. It is not a situation in which a court came to a decision on a point not argued or made in the proceedings and pleadings. Each court, in turn, attempted to deal with the point being made before them. In those circumstances, it would be wrong to accede to the submission of the appellant in this case. 

 93.               It is important to stress again the basis upon which this matter came before this Court. This Court gave leave to bring a further appeal to this Court on the basis that the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) gave rise to an issue of general public importance. Were it not for the acceptance of the interpretation of the section urged by the respondents on the High Court, no issue of general public importance would have arisen and the matter would not have proceeded beyond the High Court. Leaving aside for a moment the manner in which the appeal came before this Court, it must be said that it is not appropriate for a matter to proceed through three levels of the courts system on the basis of a particular argument and then, having come to this Court on a point of general public importance, which subsequently fell away, to change the nature of the appeal and to make an argument that had not been pursued before any other Court previously (not least of all an argument that was not, itself, one of general public importance). That is not permissible.  A party cannot obtain leave to appeal to this Court on the basis of an issue of general public importance, and then by conceding that point proceed to agitate an appeal on a ground that is not an issue of public importance, and which this Court would not have had jurisdiction to hear had it been the only question in the appeal at the outset.  But even aside from this, the more general conduct of proceedings matters. A case has been run at first instance and throughout the appellate process on a particular basis. When it becomes apparent that that basis must fail, it is not open to the party relying on that argument to change tack and make another completely different argument in the hope that the subsequent argument might succeed.  That simply cannot be permitted. The appellant has brought three appeals arising from the original decision of the County Registrar.  There was nothing stopping him from raising any relevant issue to prevent the respondents from succeeding. I accept that the appellant had made some reference to other arguments at various stages as mentioned previously, but these were never pressed or relied on by the appellant. Certainly, they were not considered by any Court or indeed by the respondents. It was only at the very last possible moment in response to a request for clarification from this Court, that the appellant abandoned the argument relied on throughout the proceedings. In those circumstances, it would be unfair to allow the appellant to rely on, in effect, new arguments made following the concession that the argument made previously throughout the proceedings was wrong. 

 94.               For the reasons I have explained above, the finding of the High Court as to the interpretation of s. 16(2)(f) is not correct but the order made by the High Court should stand. Accordingly, I would propose to dismiss the appeal of the appellant and to affirm the order of the High Court.
